# Clinical Vignette: Dr. Michael Chen

Michael Chen was sixty-three years old when he walked into the clinic, though his bearing suggested someone older—shoulders drawn inward, jaw perpetually clenched, eyes that seemed to measure every exit. He had been a respected emergency medicine physician for thirty-seven years, the kind of doctor who prided himself on clear thinking under pressure, on the ability to compartmentalize fear and act decisively when lives hung in the balance. That capacity, which had once felt like his greatest strength, had become something he could no longer trust.

The bombing occurred eighteen months earlier at a transit hub downtown. Michael had been waiting for a bus to take him to a medical conference—a routine Tuesday morning, unremarkable in every way until the moment it wasn't. He remembered the sound first: not an explosion so much as a violent reorganization of the air itself, a pressure wave that seemed to come from everywhere at once. Then the noise—screaming, the crash of metal, the high-pitched alarm of the bus's backup warning system still cycling as though the vehicle itself didn't yet understand it had been torn open. Michael had been thrown backward, his left arm crushed beneath a metal bench. He lay there for what he would later learn was four minutes but felt like hours, surrounded by the bodies of other passengers, unable to move, listening to someone nearby making a sound he would come to understand was the sound of dying.

When rescue workers finally pulled him free, Michael had sustained a fractured humerus, lacerations, and a concussion. The physical injuries healed. What didn't heal was the architecture of his safety.

Within weeks, Michael found himself unable to board a bus. The moment he approached the door, his body would flood with the same pressure sensation from that morning—not a memory exactly, but a physical certainty that the vehicle was a trap. He had come to believe that public transport was inherently dangerous, that the world had revealed itself as a place where ordinary commutes could become catastrophes. He began driving everywhere, adding forty minutes to his hospital commute, but even that felt precarious. Traffic sounds made him flinch. Sirens sent him into a state of vigilance that lasted hours.

At home, the hypervigilance had become the texture of his daily life. Michael found himself listening—constantly, without conscious intention—for sounds that might indicate an intruder. A door closing three rooms away would send him into a state of alert that his wife, Patricia, had learned to recognize and dread. She would see his body stiffen, his hand move instinctively toward his phone. Even inside their locked house, in the neighborhood where they had lived safely for twenty years, Michael felt fundamentally exposed. The feeling wasn't rational; he knew that. But knowing it didn't change the fact that his nervous system no longer believed in the concept of sanctuary.

His work had begun to deteriorate. Michael prided himself on his composure in the emergency department, but increasingly he found himself reacting with disproportionate anger to routine directives. When a resident offered a suggestion about a patient's care, Michael heard it as a challenge to his authority—an order disguised as advice. When his attending physician asked him to step away from a particularly complex case to mentor a medical student, Michael's response was sharp enough that the physician later pulled him aside with genuine concern. Michael had always been the calm one, the steady presence. Now he was becoming someone he didn't recognize: reactive, suspicious, prone to outbursts that left him ashamed and confused.

The final catalyst came when Patricia asked him to attend her sister's wedding in three weeks. The reception would be downtown, near the transit hub. She hadn't asked him to take the bus—she knew better—but the proximity itself felt like a test he was certain to fail. Michael realized that his wife was beginning to plan her life around the architecture of his fear. She had stopped suggesting they go anywhere together. She had stopped inviting friends over because she couldn't predict when he might become angry. He had come to believe that his life—the life he had built, the person he had been—was fundamentally destroyed. The world, he was certain, was a place where violence could erupt anywhere, where authority could be wielded against you, where people were not what they seemed. Even his own mind had become untrustworthy.

It was Patricia who insisted he seek help, and Michael, sitting in the clinic now, acknowledged that she was right. He didn't know if he could be fixed. But he knew that he couldn't continue like this—trapped in a home that no longer felt like home, watching the person his wife had married disappear.
